title: Dr. Strangelove
wiki_lead:
Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (usually shortened to Dr. Strangelove) is a 1964 political satire black comedy film co-written, produced, and directed by Stanley Kubrick. It is loosely based on the thriller novel Red Alert (1958) by Peter George, who wrote the screenplay with Kubrick and Terry Southern. Financed and released by Columbia Pictures, the film was a co-production between the United States and the United Kingdom.
Dr. Strangelove parodies the heightened fears during the Cold War of a nuclear war between the United States and the Soviet Union and stars Peter Sellers (portraying three different characters), George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Keenan Wynn, Slim Pickens, and Tracy Reed. The story begins when a paranoid United States Air Force brigadier general goes rogue and orders an unprovoked pre-emptive attack on the Soviet Union using all his B-52s. The President of the United States, his scientific advisor Dr. Strangelove, a Royal Air Force exchange officer, and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff luckily recall the B-52s; unfortunately, an isolated and crippled B-52 still bombs the Soviet Union, triggering their new doomsday device.
The film is widely considered one of the best comedy films and one of the greatest and most influential films ever made. In 1998, the American Film Institute ranked it 26th in its list of the best American films (in the 2007 edition, the film ranked 39th), and in 2000, it was listed as number three on its list of the funniest American films. In 1989, the United States Library of Congress included Dr. Strangelove as one of the first 25 films selected for preservation in the National Film Registry for being "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant". The film received four Academy Award nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Actor for Sellers. The film was also nominated for seven BAFTA Film Awards, winning Best Film From Any Source, Best British Film, and Best Art Direction (Black and White), and it also won the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation.

Plot
United States Air Force Brigadier General Jack D. Ripper, the commander of Burpelson Air Force Base, orders his executive officer, Group Captain Lionel Mandrake (an exchange officer from the Royal Air Force), to put the base on alert (condition red, the most intense lockdown status), confiscate all privately owned radios from base personnel and issue "Wing Attack Plan R" to the planes of the 843rd Bomb Wing. At the time of issuance of said order, the planes, flying B-52 bombers armed with thermonuclear bombs, are on airborne alert two hours from their targets inside the Soviet Union.

grok_lead: Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb is a 1964 American satirical black comedy film about Cold War nuclear brinkmanship, directed, produced, and co-written by Stanley Kubrick. The story centers on a deranged U.S. Air Force general who unilaterally orders a squadron of bombers to attack the Soviet Union with nuclear weapons, prompting frantic efforts in the Pentagon's War Room to recall the planes and avert global catastrophe after the Soviets reveal their automatic doomsday device. Starring Peter Sellers in four rolesâincluding the titular Dr. Strangelove, a former Nazi scientist with a severed hand possessed by fascist impulses, the mild-mannered President Merkin Muffley, and a British RAF officerâalongside George C. Scott as an aggressive general and Slim Pickens as a cowboy bomber pilot, the film exposes the perils of delegated nuclear authority and human folly in high-stakes command structures. Adapted from Peter George's 1958 novel Red Alert, the project began as a straight dramatic treatment of accidental nuclear war but shifted to dark comedy under Kubrick's collaboration with screenwriter Terry Southern, who amplified the script's farcical elements to highlight the irrationality of mutual assured destruction and strategic deterrence doctrines. Filmed in 1963 at Shepperton Studios in England, production faced challenges in casting Sellers for multiple personas and balancing satire with underlying realism drawn from real-world nuclear policy thinkers like Herman Kahn. Premiering on January 29, 1964, amid lingering tensions from the Cuban Missile Crisis, the film provoked debate by mocking the detachment of policymakers from the consequences of thermonuclear escalation, popularizing concepts like the "doomsday machine" while critiquing the arms race's logic of inevitable mutual suicide. It earned four Academy Award nominations for Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor (Sellers), and Best Adapted Screenplay, cementing its status as a critical triumph and enduring influence on discourse about nuclear command vulnerabilities.
